data.title: Canadian Stock Market Today: TSX Futures Nudge Higher On AI Tech Rally Optimism
data.description:
The Morning Bull - Canadian Market Morning Update Thursday, 19 Nov 2026

Canadian equities are set for a mildly positive open, with sentiment closely tied to a powerful US tech rally. Strong gains in Nasdaq futures, up about 2.3% on the back of AI linked IPO enthusiasm, are lifting broader risk appetite.

The key driver is a surge in US index futures, led by E-mini S&P 500 contracts up roughly 1.3% and Micro Nasdaq futures gaining more than 2%. That move follows upbeat demand for a large AI related listing, which investors are interpreting as renewed risk tolerance in growth heavy sectors.

When US growth futures climb this quickly, borrowing costs tend to take a back seat to earnings potential. Higher risk appetite often supports valuations for Canadian companies tied to software, chips, and data infrastructure. In contrast, more defensive groups can lag as investors rotate toward higher growth exposure.

An important question is whether this AI IPO momentum can outlast a still hawkish US Federal Reserve backdrop, with the 10 year yield sliding on expectations for further hikes. Upcoming US data and Fed speeches could shift that balance and reset risk appetite for Canadian markets.

Stocks to Watch Before the Opening Bell

BCE (BCE)

BCE is in early talks with Telus after Quebecor launched a proposed $31b offer for Telus that included a 60% premium for shareholders. Telus rejected the approach, pointing to valuation and heavy regulatory risk. Any response from BCE could reshape expectations for consolidation in Canadian telecoms. Watch for signals on asset swaps, alliances, or a formal counter move.

Vizsla Silver (VZLA)

Vizsla Silver has pushed back initial output from its Panuco silver gold project in Mexico from the second half of 2027 to the second half of 2028. Management cites revised development scheduling and is working with Mexican federal authorities on a phased return to the site. The new timing sharpens focus on funding plans, security progress, and future project updates.

Definity Financial (DFY)

Definity Financial plans a $500m private placement of 4.483% Series 3 senior unsecured notes maturing November 25, 2031. The insurer intends to use most of the cash to fully repay a $375m acquisition term loan and trim drawings on its $1.0b unsecured credit facility. The deal, expected to close November 25, 2026, gives fresh clues on balance sheet priorities.

Top Movers

  • BlackBerry (TSX:BB) jumped 5.33% after fresh QNX backlog figures highlighted stronger visibility into future automotive software royalties.
  • Boyd Group Services (TSX:BYD) climbed 3.74% as investors reassessed valuation following a recent price target cut from Stifel.
  • Apotex Health (TSX:APTX) gained 3.11% after launching APO-LINAGLIPTIN, expanding diabetes treatment options for Canadian patients.

Top Losers

  • Ero Copper (TSX:ERO) fell 11.34% as copper prices on the London Metal Exchange dropped to a seven month low.
  • Lundin Mining (TSX:LUN) declined 9.90% following weakness in copper miners as prices slid and sentiment toward the sector softened.
  • Hudbay Minerals (TSX:HBM) dropped 8.16% as the broader sell off in copper producers followed a sharp decline in benchmark prices.

On The Radar

For Canadian investors, the next few sessions pivot around retail spending data at home, a cluster of US rate sensitive releases, and fresh earnings from George Weston and Alimentation Couche Tard.

  • Loblaw Companies Thu 19 Nov. Q3 results land just as food inflation and wage costs remain in focus, so commentary on supermarket margins and same store trends feeds directly into how investors think about household spending power in Canada.
  • Canada Retail Sales MoM Final Fri 20 Nov. The consensus for September sits at 0.7% after a 1.2% gain previously, and a softer outcome would underline pressure on discretionary retailers while easing the case for higher borrowing costs.
  • Canada Retail Sales Ex Autos MoM Fri 20 Nov. Economists look for 0.7% against a 1.2% prior print, and any upside surprise would point to resilient non auto spending that supports Canadian consumer focused stocks even with higher debt servicing costs.
  • George Weston Tue 24 Nov. Q3 earnings at 7:00 AM focus attention on Loblaw and bakery results, where margin trends and any guidance on pricing power help frame how much room Canadian retailers still have to pass through higher input costs.
  • Alimentation Couche Tard Tue 24 Nov. Q2 2027 numbers after the close will put fuel and convenience store volumes under the microscope, and commentary around fuel spreads and in store basket size matters for sentiment toward global retail exposed TSX stocks.

Sector & Industry Watch

Materials and Metals and Mining: Copper slump hits resource heavy sectors

Materials and Metals and Mining have reversed sharply over the past week, with both groups giving back recent gains as copper prices slide to a seven month low. Headlines around Ero Copper, Hudbay and Teck emphasize how sensitive producers are to moves in metal prices and to weaker economic signals from key buyers such as China.

If you hold Canadian miners, the clearest swing factor now is Thursday’s US jobless claims and manufacturing survey, since fresh clues on factory activity can influence demand expectations for copper and other industrial metals that drive cash flow for this group.

Energy and Oil and Gas: Softer oil weighs on recent sector gains

Energy and Oil and Gas have eased over the last seven days after a strong 12 month climb, with both sectors down around 4%. Oil is holding near a three month low as US inventories build and supply looks comfortable, which pressures expectations for producer revenue and drilling budgets across Canadian names.

If you own Canadian energy stocks, the key driver to watch is the next set of US crude and gasoline inventory data, because any surprise move in storage can quickly shift views on oil prices and the cash generation that supports dividends and debt repayment.

Financials and Banks: Pullback after strong year long run

Financials and Banks have slipped over the past week, with both sectors weaker than the broader Canadian market even though 12 month returns remain firmly positive. Recent news from TD, Bank of Nova Scotia and Fairfax India highlights how funding decisions, legal headlines and US growth plans can all affect sentiment at a time when P/E ratios for the group sit above their three year averages.

If your portfolio leans on Canadian Financials for income, the US Federal Reserve speaker line up today and tomorrow is the key watchpoint, because any shift in tone around future rate moves can influence bond yields, bank funding costs and investor comfort with current dividend levels.

Telecom: Consolidation talk stirs a lagging sector

Telecom has been roughly flat over the past week, yet the sector still shows a decline over 12 months even as analyst earnings forecasts remain optimistic. The fresh Quebecor bid for Telus and BCE’s early talks about a potential response put consolidation and regulation back in focus, highlighting how much value in this group ties to stable cash flows and government oversight.

If you own Canadian Telecom stocks, the main factor to monitor is any guidance from Ottawa on competition and spectrum policy around the Quebecor and Telus situation, since regulatory feedback will shape expectations for future pricing power, capital spending and debt reduction across the sector.

Consumer Staples and Food, Beverage & Tobacco: Defensive group benefits from steady grocery trends

Consumer Staples and Food, Beverage & Tobacco have edged higher over the last week and month, helped by stable grocery inflation and corporate moves at Loblaw and Metro. Loblaw’s food inflation report points to grocery prices rising more slowly than overall inflation, while Metro continues to expand its discount store network as shoppers hunt for value.

If you rely on Staples exposure for steadier returns, Friday’s Canada retail sales reports are the key local catalysts, because any sign that consumers are cutting back on food and household spending would feed directly into expectations for sales volumes and pricing power at major Canadian grocers.

data.title: Will Solid Power (NASDAQ:SLDP) Spend Its Cash Wisely?
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although Amazon.com made losses for many years after listing, if you had bought and held the shares since 1999, you would have made a fortune. But while the successes are well known, investors should not ignore the very many unprofitable companies that simply burn through all their cash and collapse.

So should Solid Power (NASDAQ:SLDP) shareholders be worried about its cash burn? For the purpose of this article, we'll define cash burn as the amount of cash the company is spending each year to fund its growth (also called its negative free cash flow). We'll start by comparing its cash burn with its cash reserves in order to calculate its cash runway.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

How Long Is Solid Power's Cash Runway?

A company's cash runway is calculated by dividing its cash hoard by its cash burn. When Solid Power last reported its September 2026 balance sheet in November 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth US$235m. Importantly, its cash burn was US$80m over the trailing twelve months. Therefore, from September 2026 it had 2.9 years of cash runway. Arguably, that's a prudent and sensible length of runway to have. The image below shows how its cash balance has been changing over the last few years.

Check out our latest analysis for Solid Power

How Well Is Solid Power Growing?

Over the last year, Solid Power maintained its cash burn at a fairly steady level. However, if you like growth, you might be turned off the stock by the dizzying decline in operating revenue, which is down 80% year on year. In light of the above-mentioned, we're pretty wary of the trajectory the company seems to be on. Clearly, however, the crucial factor is whether the company will grow its business going forward. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Easily Can Solid Power Raise Cash?

While Solid Power seems to be in a fairly good position, it's still worth considering how easily it could raise more cash, even just to fuel faster growth. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. We can compare a company's cash burn to its market capitalisation to get a sense for how many new shares a company would have to issue to fund one year's operations.

Since it has a market capitalisation of US$358m, Solid Power's US$80m in cash burn equates to about 22% of its market value. That's not insignificant, and if the company had to sell enough shares to fund another year's growth at the current share price, you'd likely witness fairly costly dilution.

So, Should We Worry About Solid Power's Cash Burn?

On this analysis of Solid Power's cash burn, we think its cash runway was reassuring, while its falling revenue has us a bit worried. Even though we don't think it has a problem with its cash burn, the analysis we've done in this article does suggest that shareholders should give some careful thought to the potential cost of raising more money in the future. data.title: SMA Solar Technology's (ETR:S92) Solid Earnings Have Been Accounted For Conservatively
data.description:
SMA Solar Technology AG's (ETR:S92) recent earnings report didn't offer any surprises, with the shares unchanged over the last week. Our analysis suggests that shareholders might be missing some positive underlying factors in the earnings report.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Examining Cashflow Against SMA Solar Technology's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

SMA Solar Technology has an accrual ratio of -0.21 for the year to September 2026. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. In fact, it had free cash flow of €117m in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of €62.3m. SMA Solar Technology did see its free cash flow drop year on year, which is less than ideal, like a Simpson's episode without Groundskeeper Willie. Importantly, we note an unusual tax situation, which we discuss below, has impacted the accruals ratio.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

An Unusual Tax Situation

Moving on from the accrual ratio, we note that SMA Solar Technology profited from a tax benefit which contributed €23m to profit. This is of course a bit out of the ordinary, given it is more common for companies to be paying tax than receiving tax benefits! The receipt of a tax benefit is obviously a good thing, on its own. And since it previously lost money, it may well simply indicate the realisation of past tax losses. However, our data indicates that tax benefits can temporarily boost statutory profit in the year it is booked, but subsequently profit may fall back. Assuming the tax benefit is not repeated every year, we could see its profitability drop noticeably, all else being equal.

Our Take On SMA Solar Technology's Profit Performance

While SMA Solar Technology's accrual ratio stands testament to its strong cashflow, and indicates good quality earnings, the fact that it received a tax benefit suggests that this year's profit may not be a great guide to its sustainable profit run-rate. Based on these factors, we think that SMA Solar Technology's profits are a reasonably conservative guide to its underlying profitability. That difference matters more when Fed officials talk about more rate hikes. Higher policy rates lift the benchmark levels that many bank loans reference, while parts of deposit costs and older assets adjust more slowly, so net interest margins can widen or get squeezed depending on funding pressure and loan demand.

If you want to explore that rate story through funds with bank exposure, three tickers to consider are KBE, IAT and VFH. Each offers a different mix of regional lenders, large diversified banks and broader financial businesses. This comparison focuses on those differences.

Where could strong businesses be hiding behind a cheap share price? Explore 35 high quality undervalued stocks combining solid balance sheets and cash flows with potential value beyond the headline.

State Street SPDR S&P Bank ETF (KBE)

Holdings: 109 | In banks: 86.2% of the fund

This ETF leans heavily into banks, with regional lenders at 78% of holdings and diversified banks at 8.2%. KBE spreads just 2.2% of the fund across Central Bancompany and Customers Bancorp together, so no single holding dominates the basket. First Citizens BancShares adds another regional player that depends on net interest income from core lending. When Fed officials talk about more rate hikes, you are looking at a portfolio that ties much of its fate to how those higher benchmark rates flow through to loan yields and net interest margins.

That structure leaves you relying on how funding costs and loan demand treat regional banks in particular, because 86.2% of KBE sits in bank stocks, with much less ballast from other types of financial businesses if higher rates bite into credit quality or deposit pricing.

Not every stock inside KBE is priced the same way. Find out how many of KBE's holdings look undervalued.

iShares U.S. Regional Banks ETF (IAT)

Holdings: 34 | In banks: 99.7% of the fund

This ETF gives investors a concentrated way to gain exposure to banks that are most sensitive to changing policy rates. Almost all of IAT is in banks, with regional banks at 57.4% and diversified banks at 42.2%. The top of the portfolio leans heavily on U.S. Bancorp at 15.13%, PNC Financial Services Group at 14.76%, and Truist Financial at 9.73%. These lenders are closely tied to net interest income, so higher benchmark rates from the Fed can affect loan yields, while concerns about AI and inflation still influence their funding costs and credit decisions.

That focus means results depend on how a relatively small set of banks manage deposit pricing, loan growth, and credit quality if rate hikes continue. IAT is also more concentrated than KBE because U.S. Bancorp and PNC Financial Services Group together make up 29.9% of the fund, while Truist Financial represents 9.73% on its own.

See how IAT's returns compare with the market, from one week to five years

Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH)

Holdings: 431 | In banks: 28.9% of the fund

This ETF gives you the banks angle through JPMorgan Chase at just over 10%, backed up by Berkshire Hathaway at 8.62% and Visa at 7.73%. JPMorgan Chase is closely tied to net interest income, so higher Fed policy rates can lift lending yields on many loans. Berkshire Hathaway brings a mix of insurance and other financial operations that react differently to rate moves, while Visa leans more on payment volumes than deposit pricing. Together those three holdings show how VFH blends classic bank exposure with payment processing and broader financial businesses.

You are still relying on banks for part of the rate story, but most of this ETF is in financial groups such as insurers, asset managers and payment networks rather than lenders alone. This can spread the impact of rate hikes, but outcomes remain sensitive to how both loan demand and non bank financial activity respond.

Ten companies make up 48.3% of VFH. Find out which ones, and how much each carries.

What separates these funds

If you want your rate view to run mostly through banks, KBE and IAT sit much closer together than VFH. KBE spreads its top positions across many regional lenders, which limits the impact of any single bank on how higher policy rates and changing deposit costs filter into results. IAT leans hard on a few big holdings, with U.S. Bancorp and PNC Financial Services Group alone taking up a large slice, so any change in how those banks handle funding and loan pricing has more influence.

VFH takes a different route. Less than a third of the ETF is in banks and a large share is in payment processors, insurers and asset managers, so the Fed rate story shares space with broader financial activity. The potential benefit from more hikes relies on long term yields rising more than deposit costs. You give up some direct banks exposure with VFH, and with KBE or IAT you give up diversification for a tighter link to lenders. The decision rests on which trade off fits your goals.

data.title: Österreichische Post's (VIE:POST) Anemic Earnings Might Be Worse Than You Think
data.description:
The subdued market reaction suggests that Österreichische Post AG's (VIE:POST) recent earnings didn't contain any surprises. Our analysis suggests that along with soft profit numbers, investors should be aware of some other underlying weaknesses in the numbers.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

Importantly, our data indicates that Österreichische Post's profit received a boost of €17m in unusual items, over the last year. While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. We ran the numbers on most publicly listed companies worldwide, and it's very common for unusual items to be once-off in nature. Which is hardly surprising, given the name. Assuming those unusual items don't show up again in the current year, we'd thus expect profit to be weaker next year (in the absence of business growth, that is).

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Österreichische Post's Profit Performance

Arguably, Österreichische Post's statutory earnings have been distorted by unusual items boosting profit. Because of this, we think that it may be that Österreichische Post's statutory profits are better than its underlying earnings power. In further bad news, its earnings per share decreased in the last year. The goal of this article has been to assess how well we can rely on the statutory earnings to reflect the company's potential, but there is plenty more to consider. With this in mind, we wouldn't consider investing in a stock unless we had a thorough understanding of the risks.
